children: The crypto industry's best shot at comprehensive regulation just flatlined in the Senate, and JPMorgan thinks the fallback plan has a serious shelf-life problem.

A cloture vote on the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act, better known as the CLARITY Act, failed 49-50 on September 15, well short of the 60 votes needed to advance the legislation. JPMorgan analysts led by Kenneth Worthington warned in a subsequent note that the regulatory gap left behind will now be filled by agency rulemaking from the SEC and CFTC, a path that sounds productive until you remember that any future administration can rewrite or scrap those rules entirely.

The CLARITY Act was designed to answer one of crypto's oldest and most consequential questions: which federal agency oversees what. The bill would have split jurisdiction cleanly, handing the CFTC authority over digital commodities and giving the SEC dominion over investment contracts.

The legislation had momentum earlier in 2026. It cleared the House and made it through Senate committees with bipartisan backing. But the bill hit turbulence over ethics provisions, stablecoin yield rules, and anti-money laundering requirements. Those sticking points proved fatal when the vote reached the full Senate floor.

JPMorgan's team noted that the Act is "not fully dead" in a technical sense, since the current legislative session hasn't expired. But the bank's own assessment of the timeline is bleak. Prediction market odds for the CLARITY Act passing before year-end collapsed to roughly 6.6% after the vote.
With legislation stalled, both SEC Chair Paul Atkins and CFTC Chairman Michael Selig have signaled they'll press ahead with their own rulemaking.

JPMorgan's concern is straightforward: agency rules are "less durable than legislative statutes." A law passed by Congress requires another act of Congress to undo. An agency rule requires only a new administration with different priorities and a willingness to go through the notice-and-comment process.

Courts add another layer of fragility. Agency rules are subject to legal challenges under the Administrative Procedure Act, and recent Supreme Court decisions have made it easier for courts to second-guess agency interpretations of their own authority.

JPMorgan reiterated its support for the principles embedded in the CLARITY Act while emphasizing the need for robust consumer protections and strong capital and liquidity requirements for stablecoins.

The contentious issues that killed the bill—stablecoin yields, AML provisions, and ethics rules—aren't going away. If anything, they'll resurface in agency rulemaking with even less transparency than the legislative process provided. Senate floor debates are public. Internal agency deliberations are not, at least not until a final rule is published.

With the window for passing the CLARITY Act in its current session narrowing rapidly and odds hovering in the single digits, the crypto industry's regulatory future now rests largely on the judgment of two agency chairs and the goodwill of whoever occupies the White House next. JPMorgan's message to clients is clear: don't confuse activity with permanence.

title: JPMorgan warns agency crypto rules lack durability after CLARITY Act failure
